title: Secure Remote Code Execution Sandbox in Go with Linux Namespaces, cgroups v2 & seccomp BPF Syscall Filtering
problem: Online code assessment platforms, interactive coding sandboxes, and continuous integration runners need to execute untrusted user-submitted code at high concurrency. Naive execution directly on host operating systems exposes servers to catastrophic remote code execution (RCE) attacks, denial-of-service fork bombs, network port scanning, and host filesystem tampering. Relying on heavy full-system virtual machines introduces multi-second boot latency and unsustainable compute costs. This project builds a production-grade secure remote code execution engine and judge sandbox from scratch in Go. The system enforces strict process containment using Linux Namespaces (Mount, PID, Network, IPC, UTS), restricts CPU time and memory quotas with cgroups v2, filters dangerous kernel syscalls using seccomp BPF profiles, and executes code in under 120ms with zero host escape vulnerabilities.

use_cases.title: Competitive Programming & Automated Assessment Judge
use_cases.first_sentence: Online algorithmic evaluation platforms need to compile and execute thousands of untrusted Python, C++, and Go solutions submitted simultaneously by candidates.
use_cases.second_sentence: The engine runs each submission inside an isolated micro-sandbox, comparing standard output against test fixtures and enforcing strict execution time and memory limits.

use_cases.title: AI Agent Sandboxed Tool Execution Environment
use_cases.first_sentence: Autonomous LLM coding agents generating dynamic Python scripts require a secure runtime environment to test code without risking host machine deletion.
use_cases.second_sentence: The sandbox provides an ephemeral filesystem overlay, executing agent code with network isolation and returning execution outputs or stack traces safely.

use_cases.title: Continuous Integration Micro-Build Container Runner
use_cases.first_sentence: Developer platform teams need fast, lightweight sandboxes to run untrusted third-party pull request scripts and unit test suites.
use_cases.second_sentence: The sandbox isolates build tasks using cgroups v2 quotas, preventing runaway infinite loops or resource-hogging background crypto miners from degrading cluster nodes.

hard_parts: Configuring isolated Linux namespaces (unshare clone flags) and pivot_root filesystems with zero residual access to the host root filesystem
Writing custom seccomp BPF filter rules blocking dangerous system calls (clone without flags, ptrace, reboot, mount) while permitting safe language runtime operations
Enforcing precise cgroups v2 CPU quotas, memory limits, and pids.max thresholds to neutralize fork-bomb exploits and OOM panics
Managing high-concurrency ephemeral execution worker pools in Go with context timeouts and clean resource reclamation in sub-120ms
screener_signals: Clean Go codebase cleanly separating the sandbox supervisor, namespace isolation routines, cgroups v2 controllers, seccomp filters, and execution worker queues
Security penetration report proving complete containment across 5 attack vectors: fork bomb, host file access, network socket creation, memory exhaustion, and privilege escalation
Anti-fake verification script attempting to read `/etc/shadow` from the host filesystem inside the sandbox and asserting `PERMISSION_DENIED` / file not found

architecture.data_flow: A client submits source code and execution parameters to the Go supervisor; the supervisor pulls an execution worker from the pool, writes the code to a temporary tmpfs directory, and creates a dedicated cgroup v2 slice setting memory limit to 128MB and pids limit to 20; the supervisor forks an isolated process with new PID, Mount, Network, and IPC namespaces; the child process executes pivot_root to bind a minimal read-only rootfs, applies the seccomp BPF filter to restrict syscalls, drops privileges to UID 65534 (nobody), and execs the compiler/interpreter; the supervisor monitors execution duration; upon completion or timeout, it captures stdout/stderr, records execution telemetry, destroys the cgroup slice, and returns the verdict JSON.
architecture.enforcement_mechanism: Kernel-level seccomp SECCOMP_RET_KILL on unauthorized syscalls; cgroups v2 memory.max OOM killer bounding RAM usage.

prerequisites: Proficiency in Go systems programming, low-level process spawning (os/exec, syscall packages), and concurrency
Deep understanding of Linux kernel isolation primitives (Namespaces, cgroups v2, seccomp BPF filters, and pivot_root)

environment.os: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04+) or Windows WSL2 with Linux kernel 5.15+
environment.gpu: None required (purely CPU and Linux kernel bound systems software)
environment.cost: $0 (fully open-source Go codebase using standard Linux kernel features)
environment.accounts_keys_quotas: No external cloud accounts, paid services, or API keys required
environment.reference_environment: Local 4-core CPU with Linux kernel supporting cgroups v2, root/sudo access (for initial namespace setup), and Go 1.21+
environment.fallback_path: Docker containerized test harness (`--privileged` or `--cap-add=SYS_ADMIN`) if running on Windows WSL2 or macOS

riskiest_component.name: Kernel Exploits and Improper Syscall Whitelist Configuration
riskiest_component.mitigation: Enforce a strict default-kill seccomp BPF policy, permit only minimal necessary syscalls, and drop all Linux capabilities.
riskiest_component.fallback: Execute sandbox processes inside a secondary unprivileged Docker container layer.

out_of_scope: Windows native container isolation (Job Objects / Windows Sandbox)
resources: Linux Manual Pages: clone(2), namespaces(7), cgroups(7), seccomp(2)
The Linux Programming Interface (Michael Kerrisk - Process Isolation Chapters)
Building a Container from Scratch in Go (Liz Rice Architecture Reference)
